title: Time Series Databases — Flashcards
subtitle: 40 cards across 9 categories · Click to flip

cards.a: A database optimized for storing and querying data points indexed by time — like metrics, sensor readings, and monitoring data.

cards.q: When NOT to use a TSDB
cards.a: When you need to sort or aggregate across many series (e.g. Top-K problems). A general-purpose DB like Postgres is often a better fit.
Low-cardinality tags, highly regular timestamps, and small deltas between consecutive values. Violate these and you lose all the benefits.
Every new data point is written to the end of a file. No seeking, no overwriting. Converts random I/O into sequential I/O.
Random I/O seeks to arbitrary disk locations (slow). Sequential I/O writes continuously to the next available spot (much faster, especially on SSDs).

cards.q: Why append-only needs an extra layer
cards.a: Just appending leaves data unorganized for reads. LSM trees are the layer that adds read-friendly structure on top.
Log-Structured Merge Tree. Turns expensive random writes into cheap sequential writes by batching in memory and flushing to disk periodically.
In-memory write buffer. New data lands here first in a sorted structure (e.g. red-black tree). Fast because it's all in RAM.
Sorted String Table. An immutable sorted file on disk produced when a memtable is flushed.
Background process merging smaller SSTables into larger ones, removing duplicates and tombstones. Keeps reads manageable.
A marker written to indicate a deleted record. Cleaned up during compaction.
Very fast writes (sequential, batched) but slower reads — a query must check the memtable plus multiple SSTables.
Data being rewritten multiple times as SSTables are merged during compaction. A known cost of the LSM approach.
Storing the difference between consecutive values instead of the absolute values. Small deltas = fewer bits needed.
An encoding where small numbers use fewer bytes. The number 1 = 1 byte; 1,000,000 = 3 bytes. Pairs perfectly with delta encoding.
Takes the delta between timestamps, then the delta of those deltas. When intervals are regular, the result is all zeros — near-zero storage.
XORing two similar floats produces mostly zero bits. Only the position of the first differing bit and the meaningful bits are stored.
Facebook's paper showing delta-of-delta can compress timestamps to ~1 bit per value and XOR compression achieves ~1.37 bytes per float.
Grouping data into partitions by time windows (e.g. one partition per day). All new writes go to the current partition.
All incoming data always goes to the current time partition — no routing logic needed. Writes are naturally localized.
Deleting old data = dropping old partition files. No expensive DELETE queries scanning a massive table.
A probabilistic data structure that says 'definitely not here' (no false negatives) or 'maybe here' (false positives possible). Zero disk I/O to check.
Each SSTable has a Bloom filter. Before reading an SSTable from disk, check its filter. 'Not here' = skip entirely. Eliminates most disk reads.
~1% with 10 bits per key. Means 99% of irrelevant SSTables are skipped. Dozens of potential disk reads reduced to one or two.
Automatically reducing the resolution of older data over time. Trades precision for storage efficiency.
cards.ex: Last 24h: 10s resolution → Last 7d: 1-min averages → Last 30d: 5-min averages

cards.a: Pre-aggregated summary of raw data at a coarser time resolution (stores min, max, sum, count). Answers historical queries without reading raw data.
Uses more storage and causes write amplification (data written again per rollup level) but delivers dramatically faster reads on historical data.
Stored min/max timestamps and values for each data block. Lets the query engine skip entire blocks that can't match the query.
cards.ex: Query: CPU > 10%. Block metadata: values range 0–5%. Skip the whole block.

cards.a: Using block-level metadata to skip blocks that provably can't contain matching data. An extra filtering layer on top of time partitioning.
A unique combination of measurement name + all tag key-value pairs. All data points for one series are stored together.
Indexed metadata fields used for filtering queries (e.g. host, region). Stored in an in-memory inverted index for fast lookup.
The actual measured values (e.g. value=45.2). Not indexed — just the raw data you're recording.

cards.q: Tags vs Fields — the key rule
cards.a: Use tags for things you filter by. Use fields for the values you measure. Putting high-cardinality data in tags causes cardinality explosion.
An in-memory inverted index mapping tag values to series. Like an Elasticsearch inverted index but for tag values instead of words.
The number of unique tag combinations (series). Each unique combo creates a new series entry in memory.
When a high-cardinality value (like user_id with 10M unique values) is used as a tag, creating billions of series that overflow memory.
Store as fields, not tags. You can write them but lose all query performance benefits — no indexed filtering.
cards.ex: user_id, request_id, session_id → always fields, never tags.

cards.a: 10–100x better than a general-purpose DB when data assumptions hold (low cardinality, regular intervals, small deltas). Worse than Postgres when they don't.
A sequential append-only log written before data hits the memtable. Enables crash recovery of uncommitted data.
All data points for a given series are stored physically together in compressed blocks. No scatter-gather across disk to assemble a time series.
